My recollection is that the 2008 paper (Andreeva et al., NAR, SCOP data growth) uses PA1492 as an example of an unrelated-to-related reclassification. In SCOP 1.69, PA1492 (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, structural-genomics protein, PDB 1t1j) was not placed with nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase (NDT, PDB 1f8y). It had its own separate fold/superfamily, so the two were treated as having no detectable evolutionary relationship. They were later reclassified into the same superfamily. NDT is a flavodoxin-like, three-layer alpha/beta/alpha, class c protein. In current SCOPe the two sit in the nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase superfamily (c.23.14), under the flavodoxin-like fold (c.23). I believe PA1492 is a separate family from the NDT family within that superfamily, but I'm not certain of the family-level ID. So the change was from separate folds/superfamilies in 1.69 to a shared superfamily and fold now. The cause was better structural comparison, with some support from sequence and function. I could not check the exact 1.69 and SCOPe node IDs against the database, so verify them on the SCOPe site.

Limits on what this shows: a shared superfamily means probable common ancestry. It does not mean the same function or the same family. Substrate specificity and catalytic activity should not be transferred from NDT to PA1492 without direct sequence and active-site evidence. Superfamily membership also does not justify using one as a close homology-modeling template for the other. Separate families imply low sequence identity and probably significant structural differences.
